title: Electromagnetic Induction & Faraday's Law
summary: A changing magnetic flux induces an EMF: $\mathcal{E} = -N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, where flux is $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$. Lenz's law fixes the direction — the induced current opposes the change. A rod moving through a field has motional EMF $\mathcal{E} = BLv$. This is how generators and transformers work. (University Physics Vol. 2, Ch. 13.)

magnetic flux.plain: How much magnetic field passes through a loop's area.
magnetic flux.in_class: $\Phi_B = BA\cos\theta$; changing it is what induces a voltage.

Faraday's law.plain: A changing magnetic flux creates a voltage in a loop.

Lenz's law.plain: An induced current opposes the change that caused it.
Lenz's law.in_class: It sets the minus sign in Faraday's law; nature resists flux change.

induced EMF.plain: The voltage created by a changing magnetic flux.

motional EMF.plain: Voltage created when a conductor moves through a magnetic field.
motional EMF.in_class: $\varepsilon = BLv$ for a rod of length $L$ moving at speed $v$.

inductance.plain: How strongly a coil opposes changes in its own current.

eddy current.plain: Swirling induced currents in a solid piece of metal.
eddy current.in_class: Created by changing flux; they dissipate energy and cause magnetic braking.

concept_sections.heading: Magnetic flux
concept_sections.explanation: Flux measures how much magnetic field passes through a loop: $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$, where $A$ is the loop area and $\theta$ the angle between $\vec{B}$ and the loop's normal. It is largest when the field is straight through the loop, zero when the field lies in the loop's plane. Units are webers (Wb).

concept_sections.heading: Faraday's law
concept_sections.explanation: A changing flux induces an EMF: $\mathcal{E} = -N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, for $N$ turns. Flux can change three ways: the field changes, the area changes, or the loop rotates. Faster changes make bigger EMF — nothing happens if the flux holds steady.

concept_sections.heading: Lenz's law
concept_sections.explanation: The minus sign is Lenz's law: the induced current flows so its own magnetic field opposes the change that caused it. Push a magnet toward a coil and the coil pushes back; pull it away and the coil pulls it back. This is energy conservation — you do work against the induced field.

concept_sections.heading: Motional EMF
concept_sections.explanation: Slide a conducting rod of length $L$ at speed $v$ across a field $B$ and it develops $\mathcal{E} = BLv$. The moving charges in the rod feel a magnetic force that separates them, acting like a tiny battery. Connect it to a circuit and current flows.

concept_sections.heading: Generators and transformers
concept_sections.explanation: A coil rotating in a field has continuously changing flux, giving an AC EMF with peak $\mathcal{E}_0 = NBA\omega$ — that's a generator. Transformers use a changing flux shared between two coils so the voltage ratio matches the turns ratio, $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$.

real_world_examples.title: Power-plant generator
real_world_examples.scenario: A spinning turbine produces household electricity.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Rotating coils in a magnetic field give a changing flux, inducing $\mathcal{E} = -N\,\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$ — an AC voltage whose peak is $NBA\omega$.

real_world_examples.title: Induction cooktop
real_world_examples.scenario: A stovetop heats the pan but not itself.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: A rapidly changing field induces currents in the metal pan (Faraday's law); the pan's resistance turns those currents into heat.

real_world_examples.title: Electric guitar pickup
real_world_examples.scenario: A pickup turns string vibration into sound.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: A vibrating steel string changes the flux through a coil, inducing a small EMF that mirrors the string's motion — then amplified.

problems.prompt: A field $B = 0.50$ T passes straight through a loop of area $0.020\ \text{m}^2$. Find the flux.
Same loop and field, but now at $60^\circ$ to the normal. Find the flux.
A rod of length $0.50$ m slides at $3.0$ m/s across a field $B = 0.40$ T. Find the motional EMF.
A $100$-turn coil has its flux change by $0.010$ Wb in $0.050$ s. Find the average induced EMF.
problems.hint: Multiply the rate of flux change by the number of turns.

problems.prompt: A single loop of area $0.10\ \text{m}^2$ sits in a field that grows from $0$ to $0.40$ T in $0.20$ s. Find the induced EMF.
problems.hint: Here the area is fixed and the field changes: $\Delta\Phi = A\,\Delta B$.

problems.prompt: A bar magnet's north pole moves toward a coil. Does the induced current make the coil's near face act as a north or south pole?
solution_steps: Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change.
To oppose an approaching north pole, the coil's near face must also be north (repelling).
So the near face acts as a north pole.
problems.hint: The coil opposes what the magnet is doing.

problems.prompt: A coil of $200$ turns, area $0.010\ \text{m}^2$, in a field $0.10$ T rotates at $\omega = 100$ rad/s. Find the peak EMF.
A rod ($L = 0.40$ m) slides at $2.0$ m/s across $B = 0.50$ T, connected to a $2.0\ \Omega$ resistor. Find the current and the force needed to keep it moving steadily.
problems.hint: Find EMF, then current, then the magnetic force $BIL$ on the rod.

problems.prompt: A transformer has $500$ primary turns and $100$ secondary turns. If the primary is $120$ V, find the secondary voltage.
problems.hint: Voltage ratio equals the turns ratio.
